name: Julius Caesar
info: Gaius Julius Caesar was a Roman general, statesman and author who conquered Gaul, defeated his rival Pompey in a civil war and ruled the Roman Republic as dictator from 49 BCE until his assassination in 44 BCE.

facts.born: 12 or 13 July 100 BCE, into the patrician gens Julia, a family that claimed descent from Venus; son of Gaius Julius Caesar and Aurelia of the Aurelii Cottae
facts.died: 15 March (the Ides of March) 44 BCE, at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey: stabbed at least twenty-three times by a group of senators led by Brutus and Cassius
facts.role: Quaestor, 69 BCE; curule aedile, 65 BCE; pontifex maximus from 63 BCE; praetor; governor of Hispania Ulterior; consul, 59, 48 and 46 BCE; governor of Cisalpine Gaul, Illyricum and Transalpine Gaul from 58 BCE; dictator from 49 BCE and dictator perpetuo from February 44 BCE
facts.known: the conquest of Gaul in the Gallic Wars; crossing the Rubicon and winning the civil war against Pompey; the Julian calendar; his Commentaries on the Gallic and civil wars; the title dictator in perpetuity; his assassination on the Ides of March; the name Caesar as a title for emperors, the source of Kaiser and Tsar

t: From a patrician family of modest influence, Caesar rose through priesthoods, magistracies and an alliance with Pompey and Crassus to the consulship of 59 BCE and a command in Gaul that he held for most of a decade.

Ordered by the Senate to give up his command, he crossed the Rubicon in January 49 BCE, defeated Pompey and the republican armies in a civil war fought from Spain to Egypt, and concentrated the business of the state in his own person.

His dictatorship in perpetuity convinced some sixty senators that no free republic could be restored while he lived; his assassination in 44 BCE led to new civil wars and to the monarchy of his heir Octavian, later Augustus.
dyk: After the defeat of Pharnaces at Zela, Caesar wrote veni, vidi, vici ("I came, I saw, I conquered"). The Roman month Quintilis, in which he was born, was renamed Julius in his honour and is now July.
ev: Gaius Julius Caesar is born into the patrician gens Julia
He wins election as pontifex maximus, the highest-ranking state religious official, and as praetor
As consul, allied with Pompey and Crassus, he passes a land bill and receives Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul for five years
The Gallic Wars begin when he stops the migrating Helvetii and defeats them at the Battle of Bibracte
After a defeat at Gergovia he besieges Vercingetorix at Alesia and forces his surrender
He crosses the Rubicon with a single legion in response to the Senate's final decree, igniting civil war
He decisively defeats Pompey at Pharsalus; Pompey flees to Egypt and is killed on arriving at Alexandria
Shortly after assuming the title dictator perpetuo he is stabbed to death at a meeting of the Senate on 15 March

sections.early:
Gaius Julius Caesar was born on 12 or 13 July 100 BCE into the gens Julia, a patrician family that claimed descent from Julus, son of Aeneas, and so from the goddess Venus. Despite this pedigree the Julii Caesares had not been especially influential: their first consul came in 157 BCE, though their fortunes had recovered by the early first century. His father, of the same name, reached the praetorship and governed Asia; his mother, Aurelia, belonged to the influential Aurelii Cottae; and his father's sister was married to the powerful Gaius Marius. There is no evidence that Caesar was born by Caesarian section.

During the dominance of Lucius Cornelius Cinna, Caesar was named flamen Dialis, a priest of Jupiter, and married Cinna's daughter Cornelia; the priesthood's taboos would have ruled out a political career. His father died suddenly in early 84 BCE. After Sulla's victory in the civil war in 82 BCE, Sulla ordered Caesar to give up the priesthood and divorce Cornelia. Caesar refused and went into hiding until relatives interceded; he resigned the priesthood but kept his wife.

He then left Italy to serve on the staff of the governor of Asia, visited the court of Nicomedes IV of Bithynia, and at the Siege of Mytilene won the civic crown for saving the life of a fellow citizen. He returned on learning of Sulla's death in 78 BCE and prosecuted members of the Sullan aristocracy in the courts, with limited success. On the way to Rhodes to study under the rhetorician Apollonius Molon he was captured and ransomed by pirates, a story that was later much embellished.
sections.rise:
In 73 BCE Caesar was co-opted into the college of pontifices, a mark of acceptance by the aristocracy, and he was elected a military tribune for 71 BCE. As quaestor in 69 BCE he served in Hispania Ulterior and gained a lifetime seat in the Senate. Before leaving he gave public eulogies for his aunt Julia, the widow of Marius, at whose funeral he displayed the images of Marius, and for his wife Cornelia, who died shortly after bearing his only legitimate child, Julia. He then married Pompeia, a granddaughter of Sulla.

For much of this period he supported Pompey, backing the laws of 67 and 66 BCE that gave Pompey commands against the pirates and against Mithridates. As curule aedile in 65 BCE he staged lavish games and restored the trophies of Marius. In 63 BCE he defeated two senior senators in the election for pontifex maximus; ancient sources allege huge bribes, though no charge was ever laid. As praetor-elect that December he spoke in the Senate against executing the arrested Catilinarian conspirators, until Cato swayed the body for execution.

After his praetorship he governed Hispania Ulterior, where plunder from campaigns against the Callaeci and Lusitani paid his heavy debts. Returning in 60 BCE, he gave up a triumph in order to stand for the consulship. He won, and reconciled Pompey and Crassus in the three-way alliance misleadingly termed the First Triumvirate, sealed by Pompey's marriage to his daughter Julia. As consul in 59 BCE he passed a land bill for Pompey's veterans and the urban poor, and a tribune's law gave him Illyricum and Cisalpine Gaul for five years.
sections.deeds:
From 58 BCE Caesar campaigned in Gaul. He defeated the migrating Helvetii at Bibracte and Ariovistus, king of the Suebi, then the Belgae and the Veneti, until almost all Gaul except its centre was under Roman subjugation. He built a bridge across the Rhine and led expeditions into southern Britain in 55 and 54 BCE. A rising of most of central Gaul under Vercingetorix followed; Caesar was defeated at Gergovia but forced Vercingetorix's surrender at Alesia, and spent the time into 51 BCE suppressing remaining resistance. His Commentaries on these wars, acknowledged in his own time as a Latin literary masterwork, are almost the sole source for them and are naturally partial to their author.

Around 10 or 11 January 49 BCE he crossed the Rubicon with a single legion. Pompey abandoned Italy; Caesar defeated Pompey's legates in Spain at Ilerda and Pompey himself at Pharsalus on 9 August 48 BCE. In Egypt he installed Cleopatra as ruler; at Zela he defeated Pharnaces; at Thapsus in 46 BCE and Munda in 45 BCE he destroyed the remaining republican armies.

In power he pardoned many of his enemies and carried out reforms. The most important replaced the republican lunisolar calendar with the solar calendar now called Julian. He raised the Senate from 600 to 900 members, founded colonies outside Italy, notably on the sites of Carthage and Corinth, cut the number receiving the grain dole from 320,000 to around 150,000, extended citizenship to communities in Cisalpine Gaul and to Cádiz, and began the Forum of Caesar with its Temple of Venus Genetrix.
sections.opponents:
Caesar's advance was opposed by many in the Senate, above all Cato the Younger and Marcus Calpurnius Bibulus, his colleague as consul in 59 BCE. Cato filibustered his land bill and Bibulus threatened a veto for the entire year; a riot followed in which Bibulus's fasces were broken, and he withdrew to his house, issuing edicts to cancel the days on which Caesar could hold votes. In 51 and 50 BCE the conservatives around Cato won Pompey over to a hard line against Caesar's continued command, and on 7 January 49 BCE the Senate declared him an enemy. Scholars disagree about why he marched on Rome; his own justification was that his opponents meant to suppress the liberty of the Roman people to elect him.

His conduct of the civil war drew its own criticism. He seized the treasury by force over a tribune's veto. At Thapsus his troops massacred the republican forces without quarter, and after Munda he had his enemies massacred as rebels. Cato killed himself at Utica rather than receive Caesar's clemency. According to Appian, pictures of victories over fellow Romans paraded in his triumphs dismayed the people.

As dictator he concentrated justice, legislation and administration in his own person without regard for the traditional institutions, and deposed two tribunes who had acted against attempts to call him king. Popular indignation was likely rooted in his debt policies, the use of lethal force against protests for debt relief, the reduced grain dole and the abolition of open elections. Ernst Badian judged that he had no plans for basic social and constitutional reform.
sections.last:
Caesar returned to Rome in October 45 BCE and prepared a war against the Parthians, to avenge the death of Crassus at Carrhae, which was set to begin on 18 March 44 BCE. Shortly before 15 February 44 BCE he assumed the title dictator perpetuo, which showed contemporaries that he had no intention of restoring a free republic. Days later, at the Lupercalia, he publicly rejected a diadem offered by Mark Antony; interpretations of the episode vary, but rumour was already rife that he sought a formal crown.

The plan to kill him had begun by the summer of 45 BCE, and by February 44 BCE there were some sixty conspirators. Most were former Pompeians, joined by a substantial number of Caesarians; their leaders included Gaius Trebonius, Decimus Brutus, Cassius and Marcus Junius Brutus, who claimed descent from the Brutus who had driven out the kings. Caesar refused a bodyguard. On 15 March, the Ides of March, at a meeting of the Senate in the Curia of Pompey, the conspirators attacked him with daggers at the foot of Pompey's statue. He was stabbed at least twenty-three times. Whether he fell in silence, as Suetonius has it, or after the words kai su teknon? ("you too, child?") is variously recorded.

The assassins were coldly received in the Forum. Antony, the consul, urged a compromise in the Senate by which Caesar was not declared a tyrant and the conspirators were not punished; at the funeral he inflamed the public against them, and they were forced to flee the capital. Caesar's will left a donative to the plebs and adopted as principal heir his great-nephew Gaius Octavius.
sections.legacy:
The republic could not be resumed. Octavian, Caesar's heir, seized the consulship and joined Antony and Lepidus in the Second Triumvirate; they purged their enemies in proscriptions and defeated the tyrannicides in battle. On 1 January 42 BCE the Senate declared that Caesar would be placed among the Roman gods, and a temple was begun on the site of his cremation. By 31 BCE Octavian had taken sole control, and his masked autocracy, presented as a restoration of the republic, marked the establishment of a new Roman monarchy.

Caesar's calendar and the month named after him endured, and his cognomen became a title: it was used throughout the Roman Empire and gave rise to Kaiser in German and Tsar in the Slavic languages. The Gallic Wars, a model of clear and direct Latin, has traditionally been read by students of the language. Rulers from Charles V to Napoleon III studied or translated his writings. He is seen as the main example of Caesarism, rule by a charismatic strongman resting on a cult of personality and on force, a word that critics use pejoratively; Napoleon Bonaparte and Benito Mussolini defined themselves as Caesarists.

Much of his life is known from his own accounts, the most complete primary source but written with his political career in mind; the letters and speeches of Cicero, the histories of Sallust and the later biographies by Suetonius and Plutarch are the other main sources. Augustus began a cult of personality of Caesar that still influences modern historiography. Many historians consider him one of the greatest military commanders in history.

summary: Julius Caesar rose through the offices of the Roman Republic to the consulship of 59 BCE, conquered Gaul, and after crossing the Rubicon in 49 BCE defeated Pompey in a civil war. As dictator he reformed the calendar and concentrated power in himself. Senators killed him on 15 March 44 BCE, and the civil wars that followed ended in the rule of his heir Augustus.
references: Luciano Canfora, Julius Caesar: The People's Dictator (Edinburgh University Press, 2006)
Adrian Goldsworthy, Caesar: Life of a Colossus (Yale University Press, 2006)
Ramon L. Jiménez, Caesar Against Rome: The Great Roman Civil War (Praeger, 2000)
Robert Morstein-Marx, Julius Caesar and the Roman People (Cambridge University Press, 2021)
